message.content: The small creature's quills held the only certainty in a world that had forgotten how to be anything other than a feeling. Hedgehog had no name, not one that anyone else could speak. He wore round brass-rimmed glasses that he had found — or perhaps they had found him — balanced on his snout. He walked on a ground that was not quite ground. It was a thick smear of burnt sienna that occasionally remembered being a floor and then forgot again. His tiny feet sank into it with a sound like a brushstroke being dragged across wet canvas. He adjusted his glasses. The world did not change. It never changed. Absence is not the same as emptiness, and this world was full of absence the way a painting is full of negative space. There were no trees. There were, however, tall vertical gestures of cadmium yellow that stood where trees might have been if the world had decided to commit to something. They did not sway. They did not cast shadows. They simply *asserted* themselves upward, like arguments no one was having with anyone. Hedgehog had learned not to walk between them. Once, he had tried, and for three days he had been a smudge of brown within their composition, indistinguishable from a mark the artist had made in a moment of indecision. He had felt his edges softening. He had felt his quills becoming suggestions rather than facts. He had run. The forms that moved were not alive, but they were not dead either; they were somewhere in the grammar between, and Hedgehog could not afford to misread them. He saw one on the second day of his wandering. It was a shape that was mostly a question mark made of deep violet, with a tail that curled like a question about itself. It moved toward him with the patience of something that had never been in a hurry because it had never known what "later" meant. Hedgehog pressed himself against a patch of ground that was, for this one moment, actually ground — a confident block of charcoal black that held its form without apology. The violet question passed through him. It did not hurt. That was the worst part. It hurt less than nothing. It was a gentle erasure, like a finger running through wet ink. He felt a memory of his mother dissolve. He felt the specific weight of his left third quill from the left become a general idea of "quill." He adjusted his glasses. He walked faster. The glasses were not magic, but they were the only thing that insisted on edges, and in a world of bleed and blur, insistence was a form of survival. He understood this in the way that he understood everything — not through thought, but through the small animal logic of his body. The lenses did not sharpen the world. They sharpened *him*. They were a frame that said: here is a pair of eyes, here is a point of view, here is a creature that is looking and not merely being looked at. Without them, he had tried once, he was just another texture. Just another honest mark on the surface. He had been a hedgehog the way a shadow is a tree — present, but not *there*. He put them back on. The world remained abstract. But he remained a hedgehog. To be real is not to be the only thing that is real; it is to be the thing that remembers being a thing. On the seventh day, or what passed for the seventh day, Hedgehog found a place where the ground was a perfect, small circle of warm umber, and the air above it was a soft gradient of cream into pale gold, and nothing moved, and nothing asserted, and nothing questioned. It was quiet in the way that a held breath is quiet. He sat in the center of the umber circle. He adjusted his glasses one final time. And in the gradient above him, for the first time, something that was not a shape, not a gesture, not an absence, but a *form* with a definite edge and a definite center, looked back at him. It was not a creature. It was not alive. But it was looking. Hedgehog looked back. He did not run. He did not soften. He sat with his small round eyes behind his small round glasses, and he held his edges, and he let the looking be enough.
